## [PDF page 2]
UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland: 2005 -2024
This paper explains the 59 UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland from 2005 to  
2024, and their relationship with local government boundaries in Scotland.
These constituencies resulted from our Fifth Periodical Report which was published  
in November 2004. The recommendations of the report were enacted by the  
Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order 2005 (SI 2005/250).
A summary of the main rules and their application during the Fifth Review were:  
•  no minimum number of constituencies in Scotland.  
•  all constituencies should be as near the electoral quota as practicable. The  
electorate quota was based on the quota for England. This was 69,934. As a  
consequence this had a significant impact on the number of recommended  
constituencies which was 59.  
•  the Commission may depart from the strict application of electoral parity if  
special geographical considerations apply. According to the report this rule  
was not applied, although a: Western Isles constituency, renamed Na h-  
Eileanan an Iar, with 21,884 electors; Ross, Skye and Lochaber constituency  
with 49,544 electors; and Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross  
constituency with 46,533 electors were recommended. All other  
constituencies were within a range of 62,214 and 78,675 electors, within  
15% of the electorate quota.  
•  regard shall be had to the boundaries of local authority areas.  
•  Orkney and Shetland was designated a reserved constituency and out-with  
the review.
These constituencies were contested in General Elections on 5 May 2005, 6 May  
2010, 7 May 2015, 8 June 2017 and 12 December 2019.
Each constituency is designated as either a county constituency or a burgh  
constituency. These designations affect the allowable expenses by candidates  
during elections.
An alphabetical list of the constituencies is at Appendix A.

UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland: 1997 - 2005
This paper explains the 72 UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland from 1997 to  
2005, and their relationship with local government boundaries in Scotland.
These constituencies were implemented as recommended by our Fourth Periodical  
Report in December 1994 by the Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order  
1995 (SI 1995/1037).  They are made up of 28 burgh constituencies and 44 county  
constituencies.
A summary of the main rules and their application during the Fourth Review were:  
•  Scotland shall have no less than 71 constituencies. Prior to 1997 there were  
72 constituencies. The review retained 72 constituencies.  
•  regard shall be had to the boundaries of local authority areas.  
•  all constituencies should be as near the electoral quota as practicable. The  
average electorate for the 72 Scottish constituencies was 54,569.  
•  the Commission may depart from the strict application of electoral parity if  
special geographical considerations apply. This rule was applied to the  
existing Orkney and Shetland and Western Isles constituencies.
These constituencies were contested in General Elections on 1 May 1997 and 7 June  
2001, and in by-elections between 1997 and 2005.
These constituencies were also used for the Scottish Parliament from its  
establishment in 1999 until 2011, with one alteration which divided Orkney and  
Shetland into two constituencies.
Each constituency was designated as either a county constituency or a burgh  
constituency. These designations affect the allowable expenses by candidates  
during elections.

A list of which constituencies covered each of Scotland’s 32  unitary local  
government areas  which were created in 1995  appears in Appendix B.
A list of the local government electoral wards which cover  ed each constituency  
appears in Appendix C.

UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland: 2005 -2024
This paper explains the 59 UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland from 2005 to  
2024, and their relationship with local government boundaries in Scotland.
These constituencies resulted from our Fifth Periodical Report which was published  
in November 2004. The recommendations of the report were enacted by the  
Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order 2005 (SI 2005/250).
A summary of the main rules and their application during the Fifth Review were:  
•  no minimum number of constituencies in Scotland.  
•  all constituencies should be as near the electoral quota as practicable. The  
electorate quota was based on the quota for England. This was 69,934. As a  
consequence this had a significant impact on the number of recommended  
constituencies which was 59.  
•  the Commission may depart from the strict application of electoral parity if  
special geographical considerations apply. According to the report this rule  
was not applied, although a: Western Isles constituency, renamed Na h-  
Eileanan an Iar, with 21,884 electors; Ross, Skye and Lochaber constituency  
with 49,544 electors; and Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross  
constituency with 46,533 electors were recommended. All other  
constituencies were within a range of 62,214 and 78,675 electors, within  
15% of the electorate quota.  
•  regard shall be had to the boundaries of local authority areas.  
•  Orkney and Shetland was designated a reserved constituency and out-with  
the review.
These constituencies were contested in General Elections on 5 May 2005, 6 May  
2010, 7 May 2015, 8 June 2017 and 12 December 2019.
Each constituency is designated as either a county constituency or a burgh  
constituency. These designations affect the allowable expenses by candidates  
during elections.
An alphabetical list of the constituencies is at Appendix A.

We need list of Scottish Westminster constituencies that:

- voted for SNP in 2019 General Election.
- were unchanged (but possibly renamed) under the 2005 Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order.

So we need to map 2019 SNP-won seats to list of 2005 constituencies that are unchanged (names same or renamed). Some constituencies may have changed names slightly, but boundary unchanged? The question: "unchanged (but possibly renamed)". So we need seats that existed in 2005 and still exist in 2019 (same boundaries, possible renaming). The 2005 order created 59 constituencies that are generally the same used from 2005 until 2023 review. Some names changed between 2005 and 2019? I think boundaries mostly unchanged; only some names changed: e.g., 'Ayr' vs 'Ayr, Carrick and Cumnock' changed in 2005? Actually Ayr was a constituency pre-2005; changed to Ayr, Carrick and Cumnock? In 2005, a new constituency formed 'Ayr, Carrick and Cumnock'. That is new, not unchanged. We need unchanged.

Thus list of SNP-won seats in 2019 that correspond to same 2005 constituency names (or renamed but same boundaries). Re-check which constituencies existed pre-2005 (i.e., same boundaries). The 2005 Order replaced many earlier ones; some were new, some were renamed but similar: e.g., 'Bute' uses Argyll and Bute (unchanged); 'Ettrick'? Not.
